Management Plan
2026
Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and
Fisheries
1

PART 1. Introduction
The mission of the Directorate-General for Maritime Affairs and Fisheries (DG MARE) is:
‘To ensure a healthy ocean, sustainable fisheries, a thriving sustainable blue economy, and
vibrant coastal communities across Europe. DG MARE leads the implementation of the EU's
ocean related policies in the EU and worldwide, including sustainable management of marine
biological resources, international ocean governance and ocean observation, as outlined in the
European Ocean Pact. It implements the common fisheries policy and ensures that it is fit for
purpose, supporting Europe’s food security and healthy marine ecosystems.’
Strategic planning and programming is the cornerstone of the Commission’s performance
management framework. The Commission’s strategic plan for 2025-2029 translates the
political priorities set in the Political Guidelines of President von der Leyen into general
objectives. This process ensures institutional coherence, enhances accountability, and aligns the
actions of all Commission services with the strategic vision of the mandate.
Within this framework, each Commission service has developed a strategic outlook for
2025-2029 in the Management plan 2025. This outlook defines a set of multiannual
objectives and indicators to measure progress towards their achievement. These will be used
for planning and reporting on performance throughout the period.
The 2026 management plan sets out what DG MARE intends to deliver this year to contribute
to these multiannual objectives (part 2). It also describes how DG MARE will contribute to the
common objective of building a modern and sustainable public administration (part 3). The
main outputs with their indicators and targets are presented in Annexes 1 and 2.
The chart below illustrates the performance framework for DG MARE.
3

PART 2. Delivering on the Commission’s
priorities in 2026
General Objective 1: A new plan for Europe’s sustainable
prosperity and competitiveness
General Objective 4: Sustaining our quality of life: food
security, water and nature
Specific objective 1.1 & 4.1: A sustainable blue economy generating
sustainable economic development, jobs and prosperity (1)
2026 will see the roll-out of a number of key deliverables announced in the European Ocean
Pact, including an Ocean Act (last quarter), which will be centred on the revision of the
Directive on Maritime Spatial Planning (MSP) and will seek to improve the coherence and
effective implementation of maritime governance in the EU, serving as a single point of
reference for all economic, environmental, and social targets adopted at the Union level to
protect and sustainably use ocean resources and services. The evaluation of the MSP
Directive (2) and the impact assessment for the Ocean Act will take into consideration, inter alia,
the new opportunities offered by digital tools and the need to strengthen regional cooperation
in assessing cumulative impacts and in planning offshore energy developments, marine
protection and nature restoration at sea basin level.
The Ocean Pact also announced the creation of a public ‘EU Ocean Pact dashboard, feeding a
regular State of the Ocean Pact Report’, which should allow effective tracking of progress made
with the implementation of the Ocean Pact, and promote coordination inside the Commission,
with the Member States and with other stakeholders, as well as the setting-up of ‘a high-level
Ocean Board, instrumental in supporting the Commission in its task of monitoring and ensuring
the effective implementation of the Pact’. Together, the report, dashboard and Board will form
a framework to assess the effectiveness of policy action and to influence policy developments.
The Board should start its work in spring 2026, while the first report is scheduled for
publication by end 2026, together with the launch of the dashboard.
Through another deliverable of the Ocean Pact – the Ocean Observation initiative – we aim
to better structure, coordinate, support and govern the fundamental components of the
European marine knowledge, and through this to build a broad European and international
alliance. This is a research, industrial and cultural endeavour, leveraging the power of the ocean
(1) This specific objective is also linked to General Objective 4: Sustaining our quality of life:
food security, water and nature, as a sustainable blue economy is one of the means to
ensure food security and the health of our seas and ocean.
(2) This evaluation is also considered as stress test action for 2026.
5

for society and ensuring a long-term European autonomy in times of geopolitical change. The
adoption of the Communication is expected in June 2026. It will link both to the Ocean Act,
through the governance and coordination of ocean observation, and to the Ocean Research
and Innovation Strategy. This latter Strategy will build on the Research and Innovation
Framework Programme and, among others, the European Mission ‘Restore our Ocean and
Waters by 2030’. It will ensure a source-to-sea approach, recognising that activities on land
and in rivers impact coastal and ocean environments, and aim at improving the current
governance by overcoming the fragmentation of EU research and innovation initiatives.
In 2026, we will support the implementation of the European Ocean Pact's regional dimension,
through our four sea basins strategies in the Atlantic, West Mediterranean, the Black Sea,
and the Greater North Sea. All these activities will be supported by an Assistance Mechanism.
We will launch the review of the Atlantic Strategy and its Action Plan, and initiate a study to
assess the potential for a new sea basin strategy in the Eastern Mediterranean by 2027. We
will continue to collaborate closely with the Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy
(DG REGIO) to promote our Smart Specialisation Platform for the Sustainable Blue Economy
and to strengthen synergies between sea basin and macro-regional strategies, in particular the
Adriatic and Ionian macroregional strategy (EUSAIR) and the Baltic macroregional strategy
(EUSBSR).
We will continue to support maritime regional cooperation in the broader Mediterranean
context, working with the Union for the Mediterranean (UfM) for the implementation of the
2021 Ministerial Declaration on Sustainable Blue Economy, and contributing also to the
implementation of the Pact for the Mediterranean. Subject to the agreement of the UfM
countries, in 2026 we will start working on a new Ministerial Declaration on Sustainable Blue
Economy in view of a Ministerial Meeting in 2027.
The yearly editions of the European Ocean Days (March) and the European Maritime Day
(May), as well as the Fisheries and Ocean dialogues and the Youth dialogues will continue
to serve as central hubs for stakeholder engagement, networking and communication on a
competitive and sustainable blue economy, sustainable fisheries, international ocean
governance, marine knowledge and ocean literacy and the implementation of the European
Ocean Pact. Furthermore, the EU-wide campaign ‘European Maritime Day In My Country’
will support local events in coastal communities across the EU and beyond.
In implementing the EU Maritime Security Strategy (EUMSS), DG MARE will concentrate in 2026
on the priorities of the European Ocean Pact, namely delivering (together with the Vice-
President / High Representative) a joint report on implementation of the EUMSS, starting the
work for a communication on a safe management and neutralisation of unexploded munitions
in EU sea basins (to be adopted in 2027) as well as working on maritime awareness, including a
drone and counter-drone pilot. Strengthening maritime surveillance, including critical maritime
infrastructure continues to be a priority: we will carry on promoting a more generalised use of
the Common Information Sharing Environment for the maritime domain (CISE), with more
Member States getting connected to it and with the setting up of the CISE classified network,
which will significantly facilitate the exchange of information between civil and military
authorities, and support coastguard cooperation both at EU and sea basin context, with the
assistance of the European Fisheries Control Agency (EFCA).
6

Ensuring the wellbeing of the around 95 million people living on EU islands and in coastal
communities is a key priority for the Commission, as set out in the European Ocean Pact. DG
MARE will work on a strategy for EU Coastal Communities to be adopted by the
Commission in June 2026. The Strategy will step up support to these communities, so they can
better seize economic opportunities through (local) economic development, diversification and
innovation, and effectively contribute to climate adaptation and the sustainable management
of marine ecosystems.
As regards implementation and enforcement, DG MARE will continue to closely monitor the
situation in the two Member States, which have still not established and communicated their
maritime spatial plans, and will further pursue infringement procedures, as appropriate, until
the said obligation is complied with. The Court of Justice has already ruled against one of these
Member States (i.e. Greece) and compliance with the respective judgement and the MSP
Directive must be ensured without delay.
Please refer to the performance tables in Annex 2 for details of the outputs (page 20).
General Objective 4: Sustaining our quality of life: food
security, water and nature
Specific objective 4.2: More sustainable and competitive fisheries and
aquaculture
The European Ocean Pact confirms the importance of fisheries and aquaculture for food supply
and food security.
The evaluation of the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) Regulation is expected to be finalised in
the spring of 2026. The work underpinning the evaluation will incorporate the various studies
finalised during the course of 2025 (on the landing obligation, on the aspects of fleet policy, on
energy transition, on the common organisation of the markets and the mid-term assessment of
the aquaculture strategic guidelines). The evaluation will provide an evidence-based
assessment of whether the CFP Regulation is still fit for purpose, or where lessons can be
learned for improving it, with due consideration for environmental, economic, and social
sustainability. This evaluation is also considered as key action under DG MARE’s stress test for
2026. The evaluation will also feed the preparation of a vision for the fisheries sector with
a 2040 perspective, through which we will develop our long-term vision for a resilient,
competitive and sustainable fisheries and aquaculture sector. The Vision, which we will present
in autumn(3) will cover the whole fishing and aquaculture value chain and will be aligned with
initiatives such as the Competitiveness Compass and the Nature Restoration Regulation, and
take into account ongoing discussions on the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) as
well as efforts to enhance implementation and simplification.
The CFP Regulation evaluation and the Vision for 2040 will lay the path to long-term
sustainability of the sector and thus the foundations for the generational renewal in the sector,
(3) together with the Communication on an EU Strategy for fisheries external action and
including the Energy Transition Roadmap.
7

by ensuring its growing attractiveness. But generational renewal can only happen with a
successful energy transition of the sector. DG MARE will continue its work on the energy
transition, following up on the actions set in the 2023 Communication on Energy Transition in
EU fisheries and aquaculture and in close dialogue with the sector through the Energy
Transition Partnership (ETP) for EU fisheries and aquaculture. Results of this dialogue and
recommendations from the ETP will inspire the Commission’s roadmap on energy
transition in the sector to be delivered in autumn 2026 (integrated with the Vision for
2040).
Fishing is considered one of the most dangerous occupations in Europe. In 2026, we will launch
an impact assessment to identify the best way to transpose existing international Standards for
Training, Certification and Watchkeeping of Fishers (STCW-F) into EU law, thus addressing the
lack of harmonised minimum standards of training and certification for fishers in the EU.
More than ever, science remains the cornerstone of the effective implementation of the CFP. In
2026, DG MARE will further enhance its engagement with key providers of scientific advice,
namely the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) and the Scientific,
Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF), to ensure that they can meet our
increasing scientific needs and to address the perceived eroding of trust in science. We will also
continue to monitor the implementation of the EU data collection framework, to ensure that the
data collected can contribute to the provision of the best scientific advice.
In 2026, the Commissioner for Fisheries and Oceans will hold two implementation dialogues
on topics relevant for the sector.
The national European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF) programmes are a
key source of EU support to the fisheries and aquaculture sector to enable the transition
towards more sustainable and competitive fisheries and aquaculture, with a smaller carbon and
environmental footprint, and for building resilient coastal communities. In 2026, DG MARE will
continue encouraging and supporting Member States to further accelerate the implementation
of their EMFAF programmes to achieve the relevant and emerging policy objectives, while
minimising the risk of losing EU funds at the end of 2026 due to the automatic decommitment
rule. In parallel, DG MARE will be contributing to the interinstitutional work to develop the
framework for the next MFF, in the context of fisheries, aquaculture, ocean and the blue
economy, including the proposals for a Regulation establishing the European Fund / National
and Regional Partnership Plans for the period 2028-2034, a Regulation establishing the
conditions for the implementation of the Union support to the CFP, a Regulation on the
Competitiveness Fund and a Regulation on Global Europe.
To ensure the EU’s full and effective implementation of the WTO Agreement on Fisheries
Subsidies (phase I), DG MARE will prepare a proposal for a targeted amendment of the
EMFAF Regulation.
In June 2026 we will present the annual communication on the state of play of the CFP
and orientations for 2027, outlining our approach for setting the fishing opportunities for
2027 and reporting on the latest progress towards sustainable fishing and the implementation
of the fleet policy. The CFP legal framework, including multiannual plans, as well as the best
available scientific advice and data, and stakeholders’ feedback will underpin the Commission’s
annual proposals setting for 2027 the total allowable catches (TACs), fishing efforts and quotas
8

for the EU sea basins (Atlantic, North Sea, Baltic Sea, Mediterranean and Black Seas), stocks
shared with the UK and Norway and beyond EU waters. The objective is to increase the number
of stocks at maximum sustainable yield (MSY) level and to promote the sustainable
management of fish stocks.
For stocks managed with the UK, Norway and other coastal States, which concerns all of the
key fish stocks in the North Sea and the North-East Atlantic, the objective remains to set fishing
opportunities in line with MSY levels and negotiate appropriate conservation measures.
The pelagic sector in the Atlantic has seen many stocks decreases and the Commission will
continue its efforts to pursue comprehensive equitable sharing arrangements that align catches
with the scientific advice. Sustainable fisheries management is not optional, and, where
necessary, the Commission will assess the use of the toolbox at its disposal to defend the
interests of EU fisheries.
For stocks managed only by the EU in the Baltic Sea, Skagerrak / Kattegat and the Atlantic, and
to implement the building trajectory for the depleted stocks, the Commission will propose TACs
and quotas in line with the MSY and precautionary advice. We will continue by-catch measures
adopted alongside unavoidable by-catch-only TACs to alleviate potential choke situations. The
Commission will propose more multiannual TACs for certain EU-only stocks where such
scientific advice is available and will collaborate closely with Member States, stakeholders and
ICES to this end. For the Mediterranean and the Black Seas, fishing opportunities will take into
account the results of the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) 2026
annual session and the scientific advice for demersal stocks covered by the West Med MAP. In
the Western Mediterranean, the Commission will work closely with the Member States
concerned to assess the implementation of the compensation mechanism aimed at addressing
socio-economic challenges, while increasing selectivity and strengthening conservation, and to
ensure that the first positive effects of West Med MAP can be enhanced.
The EU will also lead the process to define the next MedFish4ever Ministerial Declaration,
setting the vision for the GFCM beyond 2027, through a dedicated ministerial conference to
take place in May 2026 in Cyprus, which will review progress and agree on future actions.
Finally, DG MARE will continue its efforts to promote level playing and fight illegal, unreported
and unregulated fishing in the Mediterranean, in line with the Pact for the Mediterranean’s
objectives.
Following the publication of the report of the EU Aquaculture Assistance Mechanism in 2025,
DG MARE will report on the mid-term assessment of the 2021 Strategic Guidelines for EU
Aquaculture. It will also prepare further guidance documents implementing the Strategic
Guidelines, notably on the environmental benefits of aquaculture and the management of
predators, and set up an EU Sustainable Aquaculture Partnership (ESAP), in line with the
mandate in the Ocean Pact. Based on the 2022 EU Algae Initiative, the Commission will
continue its efforts on scaling up European algae production, leveraging the new Bioeconomy
Strategy adopted in 2025. DG MARE will work on the future EU Blue Bioeconomy Innovation
Partnership (BBIP), to be set up in 2027.
We will build on the success of the EU Aquaculture communication campaign and continue
using the compelling video testimonials of aquaculture producers and educational content
designed to highlight the benefits of EU aquaculture. In parallel, the preparatory work of the
9

new EU-wide campaign on ‘aquatic food’ will start, as the campaign, a key deliverable of the
European Ocean Pact will be launched in 2027.
Following the entry into force of the revised fisheries Control Regulation in January 2024, and
the first implementing and delegated acts introducing new measures as of January 2026 (4),
we will continue working to ensure the timely adoption of additional secondary legislation, e.g.
on new provisions on weighing, new requirements for Remote Electronic Monitoring (REM) on
fishing vessels and traceability, and ensure that the Rec Fishing IT system for the registration
of catches by recreational fishers will go live in 2026.
Appropriate action, which may include legal enforcement will be continued, to address
situations of non-compliance with the rules of the CFP, including as a follow-up to complaints
received by the Commission.
A second Annual Progress Report on Simplification, Implementation and Enforcement (5) will be
prepared to present the progress made on key policy objectives, enforcement actions,
implementation and simplification measures between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2026.
Please refer to the performance tables in Annex 2 for details of the outputs (page 22).
General Objective 6: A global Europe: Leveraging our power
and partnerships
Specific objective 6.1: More sustainable fisheries worldwide and
improved international ocean governance
The European Ocean Pact confirms that stronger international partnerships and the promotion
of multilateral diplomacy are necessary for effective marine resource protection and fisheries
management, including a fairer international level playing field, for the benefit of EU fisheries
and global sustainability. The impact of the current geopolitical context, including pressures on
multilateralism is increasingly felt in ocean and fisheries policies. Promoting the ocean’s health
and sustainability through international cooperation and ensuring EU access to marine
resources has become more challenging, which also creates risks for economic development
and food security.
To address these challenges, DG MARE will present in autumn 2026, together with its Vision for
2040, a Communication on a new strategic approach to EU fisheries external action.
As announced in the European Ocean Pact, the strategy will aim at closing gaps in global
fisheries governance and reinforcing the EU’s commitment to sustainable ocean stewardship.
As part of the strategy, and together with other DGs and the European External Action Service

2025/1766 - EN - EUR-Lex
(5) This progress report covers all measures under Commissioner Kadis’ portfolio, also
including those that are related to specific objectives 1.14.1 ‘A sustainable blue economy
generating sustainable economic development, jobs and prosperity’ and 6.1 ‘More

10

(EEAS) we will also strengthen the EU’s Ocean diplomacy to protect the ocean at global level,
promote EU interests and values, and advance multilateral cooperation. This will benefit both
EU ocean and fisheries policies, as well as global sustainability.
After playing a leading role in securing the 60 ratifications necessary for its entry into force in
January 2026, the EU will continue to encourage the swift ratification by other parties and the
effective implementation of the Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction
(BBNJ). Through the re-launched BBNJ High Ambition Coalition, it will lead preparations for the
first BBNJ Conference of the Parties (to take place by January 2027). The EU will also
participate in the 11th edition of the Our Ocean Conference in June 2026 in Kenya,
committing further to implementing concrete initiatives. It will pursue its efforts to promote the
link between climate and ocean in the Ocean and Climate Dialogue organised in the framework
of the UN Convention on Climate Change. The EU will also encourage the effective
implementation of internationally agreed standards related to ocean and fisheries, in particular
the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the three key multilateral fisheries
Agreements on Compliance, Fish Stocks, and Port State Measures. The EU will also continue its
active participation in the FAO Committee on Fisheries and its three sub-committees.
DG MARE will support the implementation of the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies, which
entered into force on 15 September 2025, when the two-thirds threshold of acceptances (111
of 164 WTO members) was met by the WTO membership. The EU will also continue working
towards the negotiation of a balanced and meaningful comprehensive deal that includes
additional provisions on subsidies contributing to overcapacity and overfishing. Furthermore, DG
MARE will table, in the second quarter 2026, a Commission proposal for a new
Autonomous Tariff Quota (ATQ) Regulation, aiming to introduce a sustainability criterion
under this regime. DG MARE will also continue working on the impact assessment on a possible
trade ban on detached shark fins that explores a range of possible policy measures, as part of
its response to the ‘Stop Finning – Stop the trade’ European Citizens Initiative.
At the international level, DG MARE will continue to promote the EU’s sustainable fisheries
management and control agenda in all 17 regional fisheries management organisations
(RFMOs) of which the EU is a member. DG MARE will assist the GFCM by supporting activities
such as data collection, multiannual fisheries management plans, reinforcing compliance,
advancing in the fight against IUU fishing and fostering sustainable aquaculture development.
In the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT), the objective
will be to set a quota allocation for yellowfin tuna to ensure that catches remain within the
TAC. In the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), we
aim for progress on the adoption of a representative system of marine protected areas (MPA),
as well as an integrated approach between krill fishery management and special protection of
specific areas. Specific focus will be on the EU proposals for the establishment of MPAs in East
Antarctica and the Weddell Sea. In the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC), the objective is to
build on the success of the 2025 annual meeting, hosted by the EU in La Réunion, to promote
the full recovery of the tropical tuna stocks in the area. The EU will also continue to engage
bilaterally with partners in the North-East Atlantic (6) to strengthen cooperation on maritime
issues and will pursue High-Level Dialogues, such as the one established under the 2025
(6) Faroe Islands, Greenland, Iceland, Norway, the United Kingdom.
11

Memorandum of Understanding on enhanced cooperation in fisheries and ocean matters with
Iceland.
DG MARE will also continue promoting harmonised data sharing through the UN/FLUX
standard (7) to support effective and cost-efficient fisheries control at international level (and
thus contribute to the simplification agenda), including in the framework of the Port State
Measures Agreement to Prevent, Deter and Eliminate Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated
fishing.
As a DG with a strong external dimension, and to support the Commission’s strategic approach
towards our global partners, DG MARE will continue engaging bilaterally with many countries
and regions around the world. In 2026, we will organise dialogues on ocean and fisheries with
Japan, Canada, US, China, Chile, New Zealand and Indonesia and co-organise a stakeholder
Partnership Forum with China. Moreover, the EU will systematically coordinate with like-minded
countries, but also engage with countries less aligned with our positions ahead and in the
margins of international meetings.
We will enrich our cooperation with Africa on ocean governance and fisheries, following up on
the outcomes of the 7th African Union-European Union Summit and the recommendations of
the EU-Africa ocean strategic group on promoting sustainable finance and investment through
the Blue Invest Africa events and platform.
Following the President’s announcement in 2025, we will review and update, together with the
EEAS, the EU Arctic policy, launch a consultation and organise the EU Arctic Forum and
Dialogues in Brussels in September 2026.
As part of the new approach to EU fisheries external action, we will propose a framework for
a new generation of Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements (SFPAs), and
explore the possibility to conclude new SFPAs with new partners. We will continue negotiating
new protocols to SFPAs currently in place.
Furthermore, we will continue formal and informal dialogues and working groups with non-EU
countries (8) to step up the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.
DG MARE aims for the full digitalisation of the EU catch certification scheme (CATCH) as of 10
January 2026, as required by the revised IUU Regulation. This will also represent one of the key
measures to substantially simplify the work of operators and public administrations, thus
contributing to the Commission’s efforts to reduce administrative burden. Work will continue on
additional functionalities of the new IT system and to support Member States in using their full
potential for preventing the access to the EU markets of products stemming from IUU fishing.
(7) The UN/FLUX standard, developed by the EU and officially recognised by the United Nations
Centre for Trade Facilitation and Electronic Business (UN/CEFACT) harmonises the
exchanges of fisheries control data internationally and is already used in the EU. The
harmonisation of data exchange formats reduces costs and makes fisheries control more
efficient and accessible to public authorities.
(8) Vietnam, Ghana, Panama, Ecuador, Senegal, Suriname, Guyana, Sri Lanka, Mauritius,
Philippines as priority ones, and other countries under yellow and red cards and informal
dialogues.
12

We will continue to promote the system with third countries and will progressively work
towards interoperability with other IT systems.
Appropriate follow-up will be ensured to the legal enforcement actions already launched in
reaction to ineffective implementation of the catch certification scheme for imports of fishery
products, under the IUU Regulation, and of the rules related to the sustainable management of
EU vessels fishing outside EU waters.

PART 3. A modern and sustainable public
administration: outputs in 2026
The internal control framework supports sound management and decision-making. In particular,
it ensures that risks to the achievement of objectives are addressed and reduced to acceptable
levels through cost-effective controls.
DG MARE has established an internal control system tailored to its particular characteristics and
circumstances. The effective functioning of this internal control system will be assessed on an
ongoing basis throughout the year and will be subject to an annual assessment covering all
internal control principles.
A. Human resource management
The priority for 2026 will be to accompany DG MARE staff and ensure a smooth move to the
new building B-28 and supporting them to adapt to new ways of working in dynamic
collaborative spaces. Another priority will be the follow-up to the Staff Survey 2025 and
maintain staff engagement above the Commission average and to increase it further by 2029.
We will communicate to staff the results of the 2025 Staff Survey and will develop and
implement a follow-up Action Plan.
On 1 December 2025, 10 out of 21 middle managers were female, which corresponds to 48%.
We aim to maintain or increase this balance, by actively developing managerial talent in
house (9) and by keeping gender balanced appointments to middle management posts.
We will test new formats of regular debriefs from Management Board meetings and will
organise Town hall meetings with the Director-General and senior management team to ensure
staff are well informed of the latest developments. We will continue providing DG MARE staff
with opportunities for mobility, coaching and career development. This includes HR talks on
various topics, regular communication on HR issues including through the "MARE4All” Equality,
Diversity and Inclusion group, and the Greening DG MARE team.
Please refer to the performance tables in Annex 2 for details of the outputs (page 29).
B. Digital transformation and data management
Digital transformation
DG MARE is progressing with a comprehensive digital transformation programme aimed at
enhancing efficiencies and fostering innovation aligned with the Corporate Digital Strategy.
Strategic Objective 1 ‘Digital Culture’: Addressing digital skills gap remains a forefront priority.
DG MARE will continue promoting corporate specialised training on cybersecurity and artificial
(9) DG MARE co-development cycles for team leaders (2025) and deputies (2023)
14

intelligence (AI). Cybersecurity awareness is strong, with above-average participation rates, and
we will continue increasing engagement through awareness campaigns and the establishment
of a cyber ambassador role. DG MARE is planning to roll out mobile applications for fisheries
reporting. DG MARE is actively engaged with the M365 Champions network and the local AI
Champions network is actively promoting best practices among staff.
Strategic Objective 2 ‘Digital-ready Policymaking’: DG MARE is committed to integrating digital
readiness into policymaking processes resulting on more efficiency and digital inclusiveness.
Efforts include empowering staff through training on digital-ready policymaking and
interoperability. Collaboration with DIGIT's advisory service will guide policy design, promoting
adherence to Better Regulation Tool #28 principles, such as digital-by-default.
Strategic Objective 3 ‘Business-driven Digital Transformation’: DG MARE is advancing business
process modelling and automation, notably in fisheries data collection and with generative AI
tools for drafting briefings on EMFAF implementation. Despite challenges in data openness and
interoperability, progress will continue in mapping internal data assets and rolling out IT tools
for geographical units. To make fisheries control more efficient, DG MARE is developing
collaborative innovation based projects:
• Progressing with the Ocean Store, a flagship program to establish a comprehensive
data lake using cloud-native technologies for all fisheries-related systems;
• Launching a recreational fisheries app;
• Launching a system for catch certification;
• Developing an app for small scale fisheries;
• Expanding the use of AI capabilities for the preparation of EMFAF monitoring committee
meetings with Member States.
Strategic Objective 4 ‘Seamless Digital Environment’: DG MARE is committed to enhancing the
technical and strategic fitness of our IT systems. With already good progress so far (above
average), we will complete the migration of fisheries applications to the cloud, setting the stage
for future systems to be cloud-ready from the outset. We will ensure all information systems
are accurately mapped to the Business and Technical capability models, focusing on
modernising our IT landscape. We are committed to reusing business-agnostic IT solutions and
fostering an open-source culture.
Strategic Objective 5 ‘Green, Secure and Resilient Infrastructure’: Our focus includes promoting
the Digital Workplace Portal to meet staff IT needs. With an above-average cybersecurity risk
maturity, we will update security plans as needed, implement controls in collaboration with
DIGIT and MARE LISO and other actions outlined in the Corporate Cybersecurity Strategy 2025-
2026. We will identify and implement, in coordination with DG DIGIT, priority actions included in
the Digital Sovereignty Action Plan. The Eco-Management and Audit Scheme will be promoted
to encourage sustainable practices, including using M365 for paperless operations. By
leveraging serverless cloud features, we ensure applications are resource-efficient, reducing
unnecessary energy consumption.
Data management
The maturity level of DG MARE in implementing corporate data policies can be considered as
‘developing’. While all data assets have been reported to the EC data catalogue, roles and
15

responsibilities have not been defined yet; Data Owners / Stewards will be designated at the
beginning of 2026. Regarding data quality, FAIR (10) principles are being applied in several data
domains: our 2026 priority is to establish a consistent, MARE-wide approach and monitor
adherence across all data assets. The corporate operationalisation of Data Quality and FAIR
Principles framework will give us concrete steps to measure data quality and improve data
sharing. In 2026 / 2027 DG MARE will revise its Data Management Strategy to ensure full
alignment with corporate principles on data management, with priority on defining and
assigning roles and responsibilities. The objective would be to reach the level ‘established’ for
all four indicators by 2027 and “advanced” by 2029.
Data protection
DG MARE is committed to ensure full compliance with Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 (IDPR), as a
continuous effort to achieve the highest level of protection for the rights and freedoms of the
data subjects. The DG has appointed a Data Protection Coordinator (DPC) and an Assistant DPC,
who advise and assist colleagues within the DG in all aspects related to data protection and
provide regular trainings. To implement the goal of 100% of staff having received a training, all
newcomers to the DG and existing staff will receive training either through corporate, or
tailored in-house trainings. Processing operations are evaluated continuously, and records
established or revised where necessary. DG MARE has implemented administrative procedures
for the handling of data subject requests and the management of data breaches and will
continue its efforts to provide high quality and easily accessible information to data subjects on
the processing of their data.
Record Management
In view of the move of DG MARE to B28 in April 2026, at the beginning of the year, we will
focus on reducing the size of the physical archives of the DG, by transferring to the Historical
Archives any eligible files and eliminating non eligible documents. After the move, we will
continue processing the remaining physical archives and will continue with the parallel clean-up
of the electronic filing plan of the DG.

C. Sound financial management
In shared management, for both programming periods 2014-2020 and 2021-2027, DG
MARE, DG REGIO, DG EMPL and DG HOME (2021-2027 only) have developed Single Audit
Strategies. These strategies provide for compliance and thematic audits to assess the
effectiveness of the management and control systems in the Member States and to verify the
legality and regularity of expenditure.
All assurance packages relating to European Maritime and Fisheries Fund (EMFF) operational
programmes and to the EMFAF received so far are the subject of thorough desk reviews,
complemented by targeted risk-based audits for both programming periods. In particular, in
view of the closure of the EMFF operational programmes, DG MARE is aiming at obtaining

reasonable assurance on the legality and regularity of expenditure for all operational
programmes through dedicated audit assignments.
The risk related to the expenditure declared to DG MARE in the accounting year 2023-2024 is
considered limited, since DG MARE has reached an adequate level of assurance through its own
audits in the past years. Up to end-2025, DG MARE will have carried out 189 audit assignments
under the EMFF covering all Member States and will, in 2026, cover all remaining operational
programmes that have not yet been the subject of targeted closure audit work. At the same
time, DG MARE will increase the on-the-spot audit work under the EMFAF, going from 4 audit
assignments in 2025 to 13 audit assignments in 2026.
For direct and indirect management, DG MARE delegates around 40% of its directly
managed budget to the Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA).
CINEA applies its own control systems and assurance mechanisms on the reliability and
accuracy of the recorded expenditures. With SUMMA, all transactions follow a standard
workflow involving financial initiation, verification agents and authorising officer. Under the
lead of DG BUDG, HR and SG, DG MARE will contribute to the cost-benefit analysis (CBA) for the
delegation of (in)direct programme implementation 2028-2034.

D. Fraud risk management
The Joint Anti-Fraud Strategy (JAFS) of DGs REGIO, EMPL and MARE is currently being updated
(last updated in December 2019). It covers the whole anti-fraud cycle: prevention, detection,
investigation and corrective measures. It seeks to reinforce measures in place to protect the
financial interests of the EU, by providing support to Member States in their anti-fraud efforts
and strengthening the capacity of DGs to deal with fraud, as well as intensifying cooperation
with OLAF. The main actions for 2026 are expected to continue focussing on further raising
fraud awareness and developing cooperation with key partners such as OLAF and the European
Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), subject to the pending update of the JAFS to which DG MARE
is actively contributing.
DG MARE will also continue implementing the relevant actions of the Commission’s Anti-Fraud
Strategy Action Plan of July 2023 (11). In particular, DG MARE’s actions for 2026 and
subsequent years will consist of carrying out audit work to assess the effectiveness of
proportionate anti-fraud measures in place in the Member States (key requirement 7 of the
management and control systems), regularly using Arachne in the preparatory phase of audit
assignments, where relevant for the audit scope, and including in audit assignments covering
key requirement 7 the aspect of national anti-fraud strategies.
